headline: It's Fed day: a hold is expected at 2pm ET, with the 10-year parked just under 5% and oil back below $100.
dateline: Wednesday, October 28, 2026 · closes as of Tue Oct 27

rundown.h: The Fed decides at 2pm; December is the real question.
rundown.p: Consensus and Trading Economics both expect the Fed to hold its target at 3.75–4.00% today. As of Monday, CME FedWatch put the odds of no change near 90%, while December hike odds ran from about 73% to above 80% depending on the report. There's no new dot plot this time, so Chair Warsh's press conference carries the signal.

rundown.h: The five-year auction cleared 19bp cheaper for Uncle Sam.
rundown.p: Treasury sold $70 billion of five-year notes Tuesday at a 4.845% high yield, down from 5.033% at the prior five-year sale, with demand of 2.33 times the amount offered versus 2.21 last time. Paired with Monday's solid two-year sale, the message is that buyers show up below 5%. The seven-year auction Thursday completes the week.

rundown.h: Wall Street wrote a $63 billion check for AI chips.
rundown.p: A bank consortium and Blackstone are providing $63 billion of financing tied to Anthropic's use of Broadcom technology. Earlier reporting described a $42 billion senior secured tranche syndicated by banks and an $18 billion junior piece led by Blackstone, which committed $9 billion itself. It's a big test of how much AI buildout lenders will fund off contracted chip demand.
rundown.src: Trading Economics · Oct 27; Advisor Perspectives/Bloomberg · Oct 2

rundown.h: Big Tech reports into a hawkish Fed week.
rundown.p: Alphabet and Microsoft report after the bell today, a few hours after the Fed decision, with Amazon due this week. Meta's $25 billion share sale drew orders about five times the deal size, yet the stock fell 1.6% Tuesday, and Oracle rose 3.6% after widening its OpenAI partnership. Spending plans matter more than profits: capex guidance drives chip, power and data-center demand.

rundown.h: Grid and freight names posted earnings beats.
rundown.p: Tuesday's earnings mostly beat forecasts: GE Vernova earned $4.81 a share, Vertiv $2.21, Phillips 66 $14.08 and Old Dominion Freight Line $1.65, all above forecasts, while Boston Scientific and American Electric Power missed. Grid-equipment makers keep riding data-center power demand, and a beat at a less-than-truckload carrier fits the tight-freight story.

rundown.h: Factory orders beat, but core capex cooled.
rundown.p: September durable goods orders rose 1.8% against a 1.5% consensus, lifted by a 28.4% jump in civilian aircraft. Strip out the planes and the picture softens: orders excluding transportation rose 0.5%, and core capital goods orders, the business-investment proxy, rose 0.5% versus 0.7% expected, after 1.6% in August. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow for Q3 slipped to 3.4% from 3.5%.

dive.title: Housing found its inventory. Then it lost its buyers.
dive.dek: With 30-year mortgages above 7%, signed contracts fell sharply in September, even as supply quietly heads back toward normal.
dive.body:
The housing market has finally fixed its inventory problem. Unfortunately, it did it by running out of buyers. Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed rate averaged 7.32% in the week to Oct 22. That's down from 7.40% a week earlier but more than a full point above the 6.19% of a year ago. The MBA's 30-year contract rate hit about 7.5% in early October, its highest since November 2023, and its purchase index fell to 139.3 from 145.1 in the week to Oct 9.

The forward-looking data is the ugly part. NAR's pending home sales index, which tracks signed contracts, fell 7.3% in September to 66.0 and was down 11.3% from a year earlier, according to the Oct 20 release. Closed existing-home sales actually rose 1.5% to a 3.99 million annual pace, but most of those contracts were signed before rates jumped. First Trust notes that sales have hovered around 4 million a year since COVID, versus roughly 5.25 million before it.

Meanwhile, supply is quietly recovering. Existing-home inventory is at its highest since the pandemic, and months' supply reached 4.8, close to the 5.0 that NAR treats as a balanced market. The median existing-home price of $417,500 was up just 1.3% from a year ago. Builders are already blinking. Census data out Tuesday showed the median new-home price at $400,400, down 3.9% from a year earlier and below the existing-home median, with 8.4 months of supply; new-home sales slipped 0.6% to a 676,000 pace.

For investors, housing now moves almost entirely with rates. Prices aren't cracking so much as going sideways while incomes catch up: First Trust says wage growth has outpaced median price gains since early 2025. That's affordability repair, just in slow motion. But mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury, so any thaw depends on the bond market more than the housing market. Builders with margin to cut and lenders hungry for purchase loans will feel a turn first, in either direction.
watch: Thu Oct 29: Freddie Mac's weekly rate. A second straight dip from 7.40% would be the first relief.
Today, 2pm ET: the Fed's tone. Mortgage rates take their cue from the 10-year.
Wed Nov 25: October new-home sales. Do builder price cuts revive demand?

items.title: October consumer confidence jumped to 91.7, crushing the 81 forecast
items.rel: Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index, Oct

chart.src: Source: The Conference Board via Trading Economics, investingLive, FedPrimeRate and TrendForce (mix of first and revised prints).

items.body:
The Conference Board's index rose 7.5 points to 91.7 in October, released Tuesday, against a consensus of 81. September was revised up to 84.2 from 81.9. The Present Situation index climbed 8.6 points to 120.4 and the Expectations index rose 6.9 points to 72.6, still below the 80 level the Board has long flagged as a recession signal. Over the past year the index has ranged from 84.2 to 95.5, with lows in January and September.

Labor perceptions improved: 26.7% of consumers said jobs were plentiful, up from 24.3%, while 21.4% said jobs were hard to get, unchanged. Net views of current business conditions turned positive at +3.6 from −1.2. Twelve-month inflation expectations eased to 5.8%, but consumers still expect higher interest rates over the next year, and write-in mentions of prices, groceries, oil and diesel rose.

experts.who: Fergus McCormick, senior economist, The Conference Board
experts.view: The rebound came mainly from consumers' brighter read on current and expected business conditions.

items.src: Sources: The Conference Board (Oct 27); Trading Economics calendar (Oct 27).

lead.title: Tehran restates its terms as Washington weighs a post-midterm strike
lead.body:
The diplomatic shuttle into Tehran produced talk, not a deal. After Monday's meetings with Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani envoys, Iran's Security Council chief briefed Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who, per state media, restated Iran's conditions for ending the war. A day earlier, security official Ali Bagheri Kani said Washington must meet seven conditions before Tehran will even consider negotiating. Oman's foreign minister floated a non-aggression pact among all eight Gulf states, and the UK and France announced a mine-hunting drone mission for Hormuz, but only once fighting stops.

Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal reported the U.S. told Gulf allies to prepare for a brief but intense campaign against Iran after the Nov 3 midterms. The Houthis claimed a missile strike on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, which Riyadh hasn't confirmed, and Saudi air defenses intercepted missiles aimed at Taif and Riyadh Tuesday night.
lead.reach: Through oil and shipping. Brent settled at $113.88 on Oct 27, down 1.67% as diplomacy trimmed the risk premium, after a $116.72 settle Oct 23; Lloyd's List Intelligence counts at least 28 attacks or incidents near Hormuz in October, the war's worst month.

views.who: Bjarne Schieldrop, chief commodities analyst, SEB
views.view: Crude still carries a significant risk premium because U.S. or Israeli strikes on Iran remain possible in the coming weeks.
Brent should hold near $110 through year-end, up from their earlier $100 call, with shipping risk rising if U.S. naval support wavers.

reading.title: Ray Dalio: the bet that built the Principles
reading.dek: A wrong call on Mexico's 1982 default nearly ended Bridgewater and reshaped how Dalio invests.
reading.body:
Ray Dalio was born on August 8, 1949, in Jackson Heights, Queens. He studied finance at C.W. Post College of Long Island University and earned an MBA from Harvard Business School in 1973. After working as a clerk on the New York Stock Exchange, he joined Shearson Hayden Stone in 1974 as a futures trader and broker, and was let go that same year after striking his boss at a New Year's Eve party.

In 1975 he started Bridgewater Associates, initially run out of his two-bedroom New York apartment. By the early 1980s he had concluded that the U.S. had lent more to foreign countries than they could ever repay, and he positioned for a debt crisis that would sink markets. Mexico did default in 1982, but stocks rallied and monetary policy eased instead. The miss was severe enough that Dalio borrowed $4,000 from his father to cover family bills.

What he took from the episode was humility rather than timidity. He began writing down the criteria behind each decision before acting, a habit that grew into his Principles, self-published in 2011 and released as Principles: Life & Work in 2017. He also became an evangelist for diversification, arguing that a portfolio built from roughly fifteen good, uncorrelated return streams can cut risk sharply without giving up return. Bridgewater launched its Pure Alpha strategy in 1991 and the All Weather fund in 1996.

Bridgewater opened an office in Westport, Connecticut, in 1981 and by 2005 had become the world's largest hedge fund. Its culture of radical transparency drew admirers and critics alike, including a 2023 book by journalist Rob Copeland that Dalio rejected as fiction. He stepped down as co-CEO in 2017, handed control to the board in 2022, and sold his last shares in 2025. He joined the Giving Pledge in 2011.

His later books keep circling the subject that nearly broke him: debt. Principles for Navigating Big Debt Crises (2018), The Changing World Order (2021) and How Countries Go Broke (2025) all take on how borrowing builds up and how policymakers respond. The 1982 lesson is the thread: being right about the imbalance is not the same as being right about the timing, and a single concentrated bet can cost you the chance to be proven right later.

quote.text: That changed my approach to everything.

takeaways: A 5% 10-year says debt matters; Dalio's lesson says timing still humbles conviction.
Oil near $100 favors uncorrelated exposures over one big macro bet.
If the Fed hikes, size positions to survive being early, not just right.
